extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalists and editors interested in historical newspaper practice
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive historical standards and practices for U.S. newspapers (1872–1892), covering content mix (Sunday features, syndicates, comics), newsroom roles and professionalism, layout and mechanical standards (page size, columns, presses, paper), wire agencies, and labor/organizational arrangements. Useful for understanding production choices and norms of that era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunday newspaper composition
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘American journalism…has reached its highest development in the Sunday newspaper. It is at once a newspaper and a literary miscellany, a society journal and household magazine.’ Sunday editions contained a mass of feature material (literary pieces, society items, household departments) in addition to news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sunday papers mixed news with many feature sections targeted at different readers (women, youth, sports followers, socialites). Examples: entire revised New Testament reprinted (Chicago Tribune, May 21, 1887); popular songs printed with music. The Sunday paper functioned both as serious journalism and as popular miscellany.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature syndication and purchased literary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Syndicated features became important sources of material for papers; Irving Bacheller (1883) was first to set up a general syndicate business handling stories, household departments, and news/gossip letters; McClure later syndicated major literary writers to small papers for a few dollars a column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syndication made high-quality literary material available to small papers. Regular syndicated features included humorists’ columns, serious weekly letters, and women’s columns. Payment practices and the commercial availability of ready-prints and syndicated letters are noted (e.g., Bill Nye’s syndicate earnings). Use of syndicates expanded the variety of Sunday content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature content targeted to audience segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature material was specially designed for defined audience groups — youth, women, sports followers, socialites, etc. — and these targeted features were a notable element of Sunday papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors curated sections and columns aimed at demographic/interest groups to broaden appeal. This practice supported circulation growth and advertiser interest. Examples: women’s columns, youth features, sports-related features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early comic art and comic-section practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic drawings and sequences (progenitors of comic strips) occasionally appeared in Sunday papers in the 1880s; the first regular comic section began in the New York World late in 1889. Early strips were sequences of drawings dealing with a single comic incident, but usually lacked recurring characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic content was evolving from single-episode sequences in humorous weeklies and Sunday papers toward the later recurring-character comic strip. Papers such as Puck, Judge, the Sunday World, and Sunday Herald were early adopters. Placement and format varied (across top of a page or down a column).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of humor and columnist features
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor became an important element in many Sunday and some daily papers; regular columnists (humorists, satirists, witty essayists) were central features of readership appeal (e.g., Bill Nye, J. Armory Knox, Opie Read, Eugene Field, Joel Chandler Harris).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-running columnist features could sustain readership for years (Eugene Field’s 'Sharps and Flats' for twelve years). Editors used humor and local-color sketches to build circulation; the popularity could vary by audience sophistication and geography (some sketches offended subjects portrayed). Bylines were increasingly used, especially in Sunday papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News priority and coverage of major events
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite the growth of features, hard news remained primary; front pages and big space were given to major events: presidential campaigns, assassinations (Garfield), deaths of major figures (Grant), labor disturbances, wars, major disasters (Johnstown flood), prizefighting, and sensational trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers competed on comprehensive coverage of high-impact events, sometimes producing very long front-page narratives (e.g., a 11,000-word funeral story). News-gathering investment (war correspondents, telegraph expense) and editorial choices could shape political outcomes (examples: New York Times’ role in 1876 electoral dispute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter role, bylines, and professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter emerged as the key figure in New Journalism; by-lines increased (common in Sunday papers and frequent by 1886 in certain dailies). Journalism was increasingly seen as a profession with better-educated practitioners, though debate about professional status and specialized education continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of professionalization included use of by-lines, discussion of journalistic education (early university courses and certificates), formation of press clubs and professional journals, rising salaries (top editors and reporters), but also insecure tenure and rapid staff shake-ups. Examples: University of Missouri courses (1878–84), Cornell’s Certificate, formation of the New York Journalist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page advertising policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily front pages of the great dailies were clear of advertising, though exceptions existed (New York Herald filled its first and second pages with advertisements; some other papers occasionally admitted ads to page one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Front-page ad policies varied by paper and reflected editorial stance and revenue strategies. The norm among leading dailies was to keep page one for news, but sensational or revenue-driven papers sometimes placed ads on the front.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and lead conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline schedules were modest: heads almost all set in single-column measure; hanging indention and single-column light-face double-column heads were used; alliterative and editorializing headlines were common early on but became discredited by sensational excess. Leads included both 5-W’s-style leads and many feature/tantalizing leads that delayed the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical practice favored single-column heads even for big stories, with larger type, maps, and illustrations supplementing prominence. Feature leads often built up narrative rather than immediately stating facts (example quoted from New York Times convention story). Editors relied on headlines to bullet flash and allowed writers narrative leeway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard page-size and column-width practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard page-size of the period was seven 2 1/4-inch-wide columns; country weeklies and low-priced dailies often carried six or fewer columns, some columns were 1 3/4 to 2 inches wide, and some papers enlarged pages to eight columns in the eighties. A shift from 'folio' to 'quarto' (more but smaller pages) occurred at the period's end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers adjusted column numbers and widths to balance advertising and news needs (Chicago Times varied columns between six and eleven to vary capacity). The World moved to eight columns and larger page counts (regularly printing 12–14 pages, sometimes 16). Layout choices were driven by circulation, advertising volume, and press capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal departmentalization of non-news beats
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no strict departmentalization: sports and society news were treated without formal headed pages in most papers of the period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat coverage existed but formal page-headed departments were not yet the norm; specialization would evolve later as papers expanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings as investment and urban concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers invested in prominent, expensive buildings (Park Row in New York becoming synonymous with journalism). Many papers erected substantial structures as expressions of status and centralized operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentration of dailies in urban hubs (e.g., Park Row) reflected corporate investment, identity, and operational needs. Examples include Tribune’s tower (1875), Times building (1889), and the World building (1890). Such investments could also strain weaker papers financially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press machinery, attached folders, and printing capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Major technological standards: R. Hoe & Company presses dominated; Duplex Printing Press Company (flat-bed, web-feed press) and Goss Printing Press Company served smaller dailies; stereotyping became more common; the greatest improvement was the practicable attached folder that could cut, fold, count, and deliver multi-page papers at press speed. 'Double-supplement perfecting' and later quadruple/sextuple presses (Hoe) greatly increased output (e.g., Herald's sextuple press could deliver 48,000 twelve-page papers per hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press selection and folder technology determined page counts and circulation economics. Investment in high-capacity presses (prices $40,000–$80,000) allowed cheap newspapers with large circulations. Editors used supplemental presses to expand pages when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper manufacture and newsprint economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing use of mechanical wood pulp (displacing rag pulp) and improvements in Fourdrinier papermaking machines reduced paper cost dramatically: fair newsprint prices in New York fell from 12¢ (1872) to 3¢ (1892) per unit mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheaper paper enabled larger page counts and lower-priced mass-circulation newspapers. The transition to cheaper pulp, plus machine capacity gains, were critical to the economics of large-circulation dailies and big Sunday editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wire and cable news agencies, monopolies, and market power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Associated Press (NY) exercised near-monopoly power in news gathering; independent papers could not match its cooperative resources and international arrangements. Western Union telegraph company could juggle rates; competition led to rival agencies (United Press, National Associated Press Company), secret agreements, rate fights, reorganizations, and eventual modern Associated Press realignment (incorporated as Associated Press of Illinois and the United Press rivalry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to leased wires and cooperative exchange determined a paper’s ability to provide national and international news. Rate control by telegraph companies and internal agency politics shaped membership, inclusion/exclusion, and news availability. Competition and consolidation (secret deals, stock pooling) were part of agency politics; examples include midwestern secession and later reorganization around 1893.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language press composition and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: By 1892 the foreign-language press nearly doubled but did not keep pace with overall press growth; it comprised about 6–10% of the total, with German accounting for about 80% of foreign-language circulation. Eighteen languages were represented; many foreign-language papers sent a large proportion of their issues back to the homeland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnic press distribution clustered by city (six cities had multiple German dailies). Editors and managers often remained central figures; limitations in type and production (e.g., Chinese paper using lithography) influenced format and circulation. The foreign-language press served immigrant communities and transnational information flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephones, newsroom specialization, and early adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: The telephone began to be used by newspaper offices after its invention (used experimentally in 1877); by the eighties telephones in large offices enabled specializations like 'leg men' and 'rewrite men,' though instrument counts remained small (e.g., Chicago Tribune newsroom served by one telephone at period end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of telephones influenced newsroom workflow and job specialization but was gradual. Telephone availability affected speed of reporting and internal coordination; early adopters gained advantages in rapid information relay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printers’ labor organization and industrial conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers’ unions grew and confronted new technologies (stereotyping, linotype). They joined broader labor movements (American Federation of Labor) and faced employer organizing responses (United Typothetae of America). Strikes (1886–87) sought higher wages and a nine-hour day; wages and hours improved gradually though the nine-hour day took longer to achieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical and organizational changes on the business side provoked labor conflict that affected production capacity and costs. Printers’ disputes over wages/hours and employer counter-organizations shaped operational stability and the cost structure of newspapers.
